A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Jailbreak Foundry and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably, including v1 Appendices E–H becoming v4 Appendices I–L.

before.justification: v1 reports original reproductions of 30 attacks, evaluation across 10 victim models, repository and refinement ablations, and engineering measurements.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds agent ablations, trace and semantic audits, and token-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The three-component system, planner–coder–auditor workflow, bounded refinement, and evaluation harness remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1 and the appendix agent prompts. New backend substitutions and component removals are experimental ablations, not revisions to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions reproduce the same 30 attacks using AdvBench or JailbreakBench and retain the same standardized 10-model evaluation. Additional audits and cost studies examine existing attacks and benchmark samples. White-box and multimodal coverage remains future work.

E2.justification: v4 Table 5 adds evaluated pipeline comparators using Kimi-K2.5 separately as planner, coder, or auditor, plus variants without the planner or auditor. These are limited additions within the component study; existing attack and repository/no-repository comparison sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds several evaluation protocols: 15 ablation runs across three attacks, a three-sample Past Tense trace comparison, a 50-prompt SQL-structure check, an eight-criterion manual audit, and stratified token measurement across 12 attacks. Existing benchmark settings are retained. Section 4.3 also revises the reported reuse aggregation from an overall codebase fraction to a mean per-module share.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's repository, enhanced-refinement, and iteration-count analyses, v4 adds backend sensitivity and component-removal ablations, trace/mechanism verification, four manual semantic audits, core-versus-scaffolding LOC analysis, and attack effectiveness versus token-budget analysis. These directly examine architectural necessity, fidelity, compression, and efficiency.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 newly states that fixed seeds or deterministic settings are used when supported and acknowledges API nondeterminism. It supplies no specific seed values, repeated-run counts, or new confidence intervals. Figure 5's existing group standard deviations and correlation significance reporting are retained.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial ablation, audit, LOC, and cost results, including GTA ASR of 46.0 with Kimi-Planner versus the 100.0 baseline. Table 1 is unchanged, while Figure 4 adds averages and changes GTA against GPT-OSS-120B from 27.7% to 22.9%. The newly reported 5.7-point mean absolute gap follows Table 1's displayed deltas, but those contain pre-existing arithmetic inconsistencies; the ASR columns imply approximately 5.91 points.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 introduces a defined numerical semantic-fidelity score: eight criteria scored 0–2, N/A assigned 2, a fixed 16-point denominator, and explicit passing conditions. This is a limited scoring-definition addition. Existing auditor acceptance mathematics, invocation bounds, and runtime equations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central system and living-benchmark contributions remain intact. v4 corrects the headline code-reduction claim from 42% to 58%, consistent with the unchanged LOC totals, and qualifies the 82.5% reuse figure as a mean per-module share rather than a fraction of the entire integrated codebase.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly distinguishes ASR agreement from semantic fidelity, repository compression from fidelity, and attack effectiveness from budget efficiency. It adds interpretations of planner sensitivity and concrete limitations concerning manual framework extension, text-only black/gray-box coverage, and adversarial papers or repositories affecting the agents. These substantially qualify the system's applicability and evidence.

D1.justification: New disclosures include ABJ's gpt-4o-mini assist-model substitution, ReNeLLM's fixed 0.5 temperature, and stage-specific total and cached token usage. These document implementation choices and resource requirements without establishing changes between implementations. Existing interfaces, full agent prompts, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds reproducibility and peer-review context supported by Gundersen et al., Raff et al., and Aczel et al. This broadens the motivation modestly while retaining the same positioning around automated attack integration and standardized evaluation.

P1.justification: v4 locally expands the paper-to-code discussion, adds a randomness paragraph, clarifies reuse wording, and extends future work. New analytical appendices are inserted and existing appendices renumbered, but the main narrative structure, method exposition, and full agent instructions are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 3–8 displaying token costs, ablations, traces, semantic scores, and core LOC, plus Figure 6's budget-effectiveness scatterplot. Figure 4 is redrawn with attack/model averages and reordered columns, and Figure 3's legend typo is corrected. This substantially expands the visual presentation of the evidence.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design and fidelity claims through component ablations and checks beyond aggregate ASR. Cost analyses, corrected compression reporting, and explicit applicability and security limitations also improve assessability. Small selected audit samples, absent repeated-run uncertainty, and remaining numerical inconsistencies limit confidence, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.
